bilingual.notes: Bilingual Education endorsement governed by PESB under WAC 181-82A. Added to a teaching certificate (no standalone license). Per WAC 181-82A-204(2)(a), the route is a state-approved endorsement program addressing PESB competencies plus the WEST-E content test; field experience is at the program provider's discretion. PESB endorsement competencies (Standard 1.A) require candidates to demonstrate 'a high level of oral and written language proficiency' in the additional language of instruction 'as demonstrated by performance on a standardized assessment of language proficiency.' Post-Fall 2021 candidates are evaluated against NDLETPS (National Dual Language Education Teacher Preparation Standards).

eld.notes: English Language Learner (ELL) endorsement (PESB, 2015 competencies). Added to a teaching certificate (no standalone license). Same WAC 181-82A-204 route as Bilingual: state-approved endorsement program plus WEST-E content test; field experience at provider discretion. Unlike the Bilingual endorsement, no candidate language-proficiency gate. OSPI uses 'Multilingual/English Learner' branding in current program guidance; PESB retains the 'ELL' label on the endorsement itself.

sei.notes: Washington has no universal SEI / sheltered-instruction endorsement mandate. The Transitional Bilingual Instruction Program (TBIP, RCW 28A.180) is an OSPI-administered district program serving identified multilingual/EL students; it does not require all certificated teachers to hold an EL-related endorsement.

history.title: Washington Transitional Bilingual Instruction Program established (Ch. 95, Laws of 1979)
history.description: The Washington Legislature enacted RCW 28A.180 (originally Chapter 95, Laws of 1979) creating the Transitional Bilingual Instruction Program (TBIP) and committing state funds to districts serving EL students. Unlike the bilingual mandates in MA/NM/TX/IL/NJ, Washington's statute permits districts to choose program model — bilingual where staffing allows, ESL/sheltered instruction otherwise — and ties state funding to enrollment of identified ELs. RCW 28A.180.020 still requires OSPI to report annually on the program. OSPI rebranded the umbrella as the Multilingual Education Program in recent guidance, but the underlying TBIP statute remains the legal backbone of WA's EL services.

history.title: EPAA 29(100) document analysis (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021)
history.description: Leider, Colombo & Nerlino published in Education Policy Analysis Archives 29(100) a comprehensive document analysis of every state and DC's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI teacher-credentialing requirements, professional teaching standards mentions, and EL-percentage figures, based on primary SEA sources collected October–December 2019. The 2019 coding of Washington's EL-credentialing landscape is preserved as a temporally-anchored research baseline against which the catalog's later verifications are framed.

elPercentHistory.note: Washington Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction, October 1 fall snapshot (167,665 Multilingual Learners). Washington's terminology shifted from "English Learner" to "Multilingual Learner" around 2022-23; OSPI guidance on whether the definitional change altered the counted population is not explicit in available sources. The 3.7 percentage-point increase from NCES's fall 2021 value (11.4%) is large; without a directly comparable OSPI-published series for the NCES overlap years, methodological continuity cannot be confirmed from overlapping observations. Part of the gap reflects documented enrollment growth from 2022-23 (13.4%) to 2024-25 (15.1%).
